bloks.name: STRAIGHT UP
bloks.title: Chaos Is a Ladder
bloks.dek: Before you climb anything, know your emotional triggers.

body.text: Chaos is a ladder — but before you climb anything, know your emotional triggers.
When you swim with chaos rather than fight it, you minimize how much of it gets to you.
“Cut out the bad bits.”
—Walter Murch
The hard part? No one cheers you on when you make the preventative, composed choice.
In fact, the applause tends to go the other way — toward outbursts, gossip, and emotional performance, misreading attention as growth.

body.alt: “Chaos is a ladder” GIF from Game of Thrones

body.text: Film editor Walter Murch once described the editing process simply: “Cut out the bad bits.”¹
Do that — honest self-editing — and you become comfortable in chaos, patiently finding opportunities instead of reacting to nonsensical noise.
¹ Book reference: “In the Blink of an Eye” by Walter Murch.

bloks.title: I Guess Monopolies Are Fine Now 🤷‍♂️
bloks.dek: UMG swallows Downtown Music, and indies took a hit.

body.text: She goes by Miss Krystle — lawyer, YouTuber, and musician — and she’s out here fighting for the little guy/girl.

body.cap: Miss Krystle on UMG and Downtown Music. Watch on YouTube.

body.text: In this video she breaks down Universal Music Group’s acquisition of Downtown Music Holdings, a $775 million deal that just closed last month after a lengthy regulatory battle with the European Commission.
The EU approved it — but only after forcing UMG to spin off Curve, Downtown’s royalty and rights-management platform, which gave them access to sensitive data from hundreds of independent labels.
Downtown’s catalog includes CD Baby, FUGA, and Songtrust. UMG is already the largest record label on the planet. You do the math.
Miss Krystle does it for you.

bloks.name: WORD MEME
bloks.title: F Elon: A Historic Bait and Switch

body.text: Elon Musk, just in general, is kind of cringe.
I mean that in the most observational way possible — because he’s also the kind of character that will probably get chiseled into a mountain somewhere. That’s what makes him interesting to study.
The “F Elon” meme didn’t come from nowhere. It was born out of a very specific bait-and-switch — an ideological one.

Tesla was sold, consciously or not, as a certain kind of product for a certain kind of person. Clean energy. Innovation. A better future. A lot of people bought in — literally, by way of cars and unprecedented brand loyalty.
Then the curtain pulled back.

body.alt: A black T-shirt mockup reading F ELON over a starship graphic.

body.text: What you actually got was: a chosen technocrat, the new Steve Jobs (his words, essentially), a 14-kid-having, DOGE-leading, SpaceX-and-Tesla-running character who it turns out was never the progressive green-tech savior anyone projected onto him.
He was always something else. The projection was the problem.
And now the cope is in full form.

The “I bought this before Elon went crazy” bumper sticker is one of the more honest artifacts of recent cultural history. It’s an apology and a disclaimer at the same time. A little white flag stuck to the back of a $50,000 car.

body.alt: Bumper sticker: I bought this before Elon went crazy.

body.text: No offense — genuinely — but this is a learning moment for everyone. You can drink the Kool-Aid on a brand, a person, a movement, without ever really looking underneath. And when the floor drops, the surprise feels personal.
Maybe it’s just the old “never meet your heroes” rule — or maybe it’s what happens when you let marketing campaigns do the work that research was supposed to do.
Enter: F Elon.
First spotted — by me — as a bumper sticker in a sci-fi, Blade Runner-adjacent font: clean, aggressive, and committed.

body.alt: The F ELON bumper sticker in a sci-fi font.

body.text: There’s the obvious read. Then there’s the second layer: felon — an individual found guilty of a felony offense. Whether that second meaning is intentional or just an extremely fortunate accident of language, it doesn’t matter. The meme works because both meanings land simultaneously.
I made clothing mockups, an original video, and a song inspired by this moment in history. Enjoy.

bloks.name: FIND YOUR EDGE
bloks.title: Age Called. He Didn’t Pick Up.
bloks.dek: At 70, Michael Kish ran the 100m in 13.47 seconds.

body.text: Age comes up a lot — usually from two kinds of people: those under 30 who can’t imagine it yet, and those who’ve already talked themselves into a ceiling.
People use age to judge, qualify, and put you in your proverbial place. Michael Kish didn’t get the memo.
At 70, he ran the 100m at the Penn Relays in 13.47 seconds — faster than the winning time in the 65-and-over division. He pulled away from the gun and never looked back.
Age is just age. The rest is a story you’re telling yourself.

body.cap: Michael Kish, 70, runs the 100m. Watch on YouTube.

bloks.title: Men’s Fragrance 101
bloks.dek: Three entry points for the guy who’s never really thought about it.

body.text: This one’s for the guys who’ve never really thought about it — and for the women who’ve been waiting for their man to figure it out. Feel free to forward this section accordingly.
Fragrance is one of the most underrated tools in a man’s arsenal. It’s invisible, immediate, and says something about you before you even enter the room.
Getting started is easier than it looks.
The video below gives you a solid contextual framework to start navigating it.

body.cap: A man’s introduction to fragrance. Watch on YouTube.

body.text: Here are three entry points worth knowing:
1. Acqua Di Gio by Giorgio Armani
Light, aquatic, with a touch of citrus. A genuine all-purpose fragrance, especially in warmer months. Hard to go wrong here.

body.label: Shop Acqua Di Gio at Nordstrom →

body.text: 2. Burberry Hero
⭐️ my favorite ⭐️ Understated and woodsy with a hint of bergamot. Leans into a masculine frame without begging for attention. This one wears quietly and confidently.
3. Gucci Guilty
Lemon, pink pepper, cedar, lavender, mandarin, and crushed green leaves. A lot going on in the best way — makes it a great everyday statement wear without being overpowering.
Start with one. You’ll understand why it matters the first time someone notices.
Since Issue 1, this newsletter has been quietly building a crypto foundation — brick by brick.

We opened with the original cypherpunk principles: why crypto was born, what it was actually for, and why the people behind it weren’t just tech nerds but ideological dissenters from a financial system they didn’t trust.

Then came Yonatan Sompolinsky — the math guy behind Kaspa, whose earlier work on GHOST protocol was cited in Ethereum’s own whitepaper, and who most people still haven’t heard of. We broke down what Kaspa actually is — first in playground metaphors, then in plain terms. Speed without sacrificing the decentralization and security that make the whole thing mean something.
That’s the foundation. Now the harder conversation.
The State of Play

This isn’t a down year. This isn’t the dog days. For anyone who joined the crypto system in the last four or five years, this has been an absolute financial dumpster fire. And the strange part is — crypto is everywhere in the headlines.

Stablecoins are crypto. Tom Lee’s BitMine just invested $9 billion into Ethereum and other assets, planting a flag that looks a lot like a long-term conviction bet. Bitcoin and Ethereum now have Wall Street ETFs. The infrastructure is being built.
And yet — most people still don’t really understand what any of it is.

Is it a new financial system? A network of digital communities organized around shared protocols? Is it outside the traditional financial system or now inside it? Are crypto projects just elaborate scams? Is there genuine innovation? Real utility? Are these things commodities, currencies, or something closer to stocks?
If you answered yes to all of that — you’re actually not wrong.

Here’s the honest read: crypto is currently in its believer stage. Either you believe in it or you don’t. There’s a real possibility it all fails. But there’s also the feeling that its roots are already too deep in the culture and the capital markets to fully disappear.
The Bid Problem

The core financial problem right now is that most crypto projects can’t hold a bid. That means there isn’t enough sustained buying activity to keep prices stable, let alone growing. They keep falling. The main culprit is trust — or the lack of it. The risk feels too high, the timeline too uncertain, and too many people have been burned to feel comfortable leaving money in.
But zoom out, and the picture gets more interesting.

Crypto has always been, at its heart, a retail phenomenon. It moves on emotion. And right now, retail — the everyday investor, Main Street — is wrecked. Everything we bought five or six years ago costs roughly double. Wages didn’t double. Savings didn’t double. The gap between what things cost and what people actually have is widening in ways that are hard to look at directly.
And here’s where crypto was supposed to be the answer — and why so many people flocked to it in the first place.
Dollar Debasement

When a government prints money at scale, the value of every dollar (or any other nationalized unit of currency) already in circulation quietly shrinks. It’s inflation’s quieter cousin — less visible, more systemic. Crypto, Bitcoin especially, was built as a direct response to that: a fixed supply, no central authority, no printing press. The pitch was sound money for a world that had stopped trusting fiat.

The irony is brutal: the very conditions that justified crypto’s existence are now the same conditions making it hard for regular people to stay in it. When your rent is up 40% and your grocery bill is up 30%, you don’t leave money sitting in volatile assets hoping for a ten-year payoff. You pull it out.
The pain of being early and called stupid. That’s the price of entry for asymmetric upside.
Where We Stand
The problems crypto is trying to solve are real. But trust — in the projects, in the people running them, in the timeline — is still being sorted out.
Crypto’s allure, beyond the technology, was being early to a new capitalistic frontier. It’s not quite like anything we’ve seen before — part investment, part digital community, part ideology.
If we knew where this was heading, the payout would be low. That’s what government bonds are for — parking money in an instrument that pays 3–5% with near certainty.
Crypto offers no such certainty: the volatility, the not knowing, the pain of being early and called stupid. That’s the price of entry for asymmetric upside.
Whether that price buys protection from dollar debasement, inflation, and a broken job market remains the question. We’re invested in the answer.

bloks.name: MUSIC FLOW
bloks.title: Omido’s “LSD” and a Stunning Video to Match
bloks.dek: One continuous dance performance. No cuts.

body.text: If you haven’t seen this one yet, get ready.

Omido is an Austrian producer and DJ who makes slow, organic, guitar-influenced electronic music that doesn’t sound like anything else in the space. He grew up on metal, got lost in drum and bass, then picked the guitar back up and built something entirely his own.
“LSD” is the result. The song itself is a melodramatic electronic love ballad about knowing better and falling anyway.
But the video is what makes it a comprehensive classic:
One continuous dance performance shot through a remote woodsy house. No cuts, no production tricks — just movement, space, and the song doing its job.
It’s been five years and it doesn’t get old.

bloks.name: NOW PLAYING
bloks.title: Snowpiercer’s Unlikely Masterpiece Has a Portishead Heart
bloks.dek: A TV show based on a film, and surprisingly impressive.

body.text: Here’s the TL;DR upfront: Snowpiercer is a TV show based on a film, and it’s surprisingly impressive. Jennifer Connelly carries the show with her talent and understated star power. There are riveting moments throughout — including several live musical performances built directly into the plot.
One of them is a cover of Portishead’s “Glory Box.” 🗺️ Treasure Hunt: the answer is on the Back Page.

body.label: 🗺️ Jump to the Treasure Hunt answer →

body.text: Portishead is a late ’90s trip-hop group from Bristol — textured, down-tempo, cinematic, and built around the voice of Beth Gibbons, who sounds like she’s singing from somewhere most people aren’t allowed to go.

Funny story: I used to play their albums on repeat way back when, and most people either didn’t know who they were or, worse, made fun of me for listening — calling me weird and saying it was “too dark.” And now? It’s completely normal to love this band.

The ’90s are having a full glow-up moment in culture right now — things that were considered niche or strange are getting the recognition they deserved all along, just twenty-plus years late. Portishead is one of those.

The show itself works surprisingly well given how unlikely the premise sounds — a world where a climate intervention goes catastrophically wrong and freezes the planet. The last survivors live on a massive train that never stops moving. A class-based society forms, followed by a fascinating portrayal of struggle, politics, and violence. It’s genuinely well-executed, especially considering how easily such an ambitious concept could have failed. Though fair warning: it is quite violent.

The scene in this clip features the Glory Box cover performed by Miss Audrey (played by Lena Hall), who runs the train’s nightclub. She sings it to the show’s main antagonist, Joseph Wilford (played by Sean Bean) — and she, not entirely by choice, was once something like his girlfriend.
The song really hits different when you understand what’s underneath it (the plot dynamics and the Portishead homage).
